source: Macnamara & Hambrick (2020) Is the deliberate practice view defensible? A review of evidence and discussion of issues
finding: Post-corrigendum summary of the 2014 meta-analysis. Overall deliberate practice explained 14% of variance (r = 0.38), not 12% (r = .35). Domain split moved up a little. Closes gap 4.
numbers: 88 studies; 14% overall; games 24%, music 23%, sports 20%, education 5%, professions 1%. Authors state their r = 0.38 vs Miller et al. reanalysis r = 0.40 (non-deliberate practice r = 0.21). Cites the Macnamara 2018 corrigendum.
quote: deliberate practice explained 14% of the variance in performance overall, and 24% for games, 23% for music, 20% for sports, 5% for education, and 1% for professions
limits: Read in full via PMC. The corrigendum itself (Psych Sci 29(7):1202-1204) is paywalled; figures are the authors' own later citation. The 2014 abstract's 26/21/18/4/<1 are superseded.
agent_relevance: Background only. Use 14% overall, 20-24% in rule-bound domains.

source: Macnamara & Hambrick (2020) review, reliability and correction section
finding: The corrected r=.61 rests on an ASSUMED reliability of 0.80 for practice, taken from two Ericsson-camp statements, not from direct measurement. Lower assumed reliability gives a bigger correction.
numbers: Chess raw r = .49, music raw r = .43. Reliable variance explained: chess 34%, music 29.9% (E&H 2019 numbers as quoted). Gobet & Campitelli 2007: N=90 chess players, practice-rating r = .42; hours to reach master ranged 3,016 to 23,608 (factor of about 8).
quote: we assumed a reliability coefficient of 0.80
limits: Secondary account of a rival camp's method. Gap 5 partly closed: the assumption is documented, direct long-interval reliability is still unmeasured.
agent_relevance: None for agent. Corrections depend on unmeasured inputs.

source: Ericsson & Harwell (2019) Deliberate practice and proposed limits on the effects of practice on the acquisition of expert performance
finding: Direct reliability evidence for retrospective practice estimates is thin and short-interval. Musicians and chess players recall current-year weekly hours at r .60-.75; for 15-20 years back it is plausibly lower. Authors adopt 0.6 for the correction.
numbers: de Bruin et al. 2008 chess diary vs weekly estimate r(34)=.60; musicians diary vs estimate .60-.75; leisure estimates r(28)=.082 (not reliable). Ward et al. 2007: estimates reliable only for the last 5 years, older years not significantly correlated. Baker et al. 2003 athlete vs parent r=.59, p<.05.
quote: There have not been any studies that have collected concurrent diary data on weekly practice for aspiring experts throughout their entire development.
limits: The authors themselves say the full-career figure is a guess (0.6). Gap 5 stays open for full careers. Recall bias direction unknown.

source: Macnamara & Hambrick (2020) review, elite samples, range restriction, chess fluid intelligence
finding: Nobody has run a range-restriction correction on elite-only samples. Both camps concede restriction lowers r among elites; they dispute what the 1993 text implied. Gap 6 stays open.
numbers: Elite athletes (national level and up): practice explained 1% of variance (2016 sports meta). Burgoyne chess meta-analysis: fluid intelligence r = .32 in lower-skill vs .14 in higher-skill players, but skill is confounded with age (youth vs adult samples).
quote: range restriction (another psychometric issue) would limit the deliberate practice-performance correlation when considering only elite performers
limits: Sports figure is the 2016 meta; no new test. Chess split is confounded.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald (2018) Corrigendum: Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions
finding: Record of the 2014 meta-analysis corrigendum: Psychological Science 29(7):1202-1204, published 2018-05-07, typed as erratum for the 2014 paper.
numbers: Metadata only (Europe PMC id 29733772). Corrected values not read here; taken from d01.
limits: Text not opened: the SAGE PDF returned an HTML block page. Only the Europe PMC record was read.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) SPEED-RL: Faster training of reasoning models via online curriculum learning
finding: Filtering to mid-pass-rate prompts speeds RL 2-6x in wall-clock time to a target accuracy, with screening cost counted. Gradient SNR theory says prompts at 0% or 100% pass rate give near-zero signal.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and 7B; RLOO and DAPO; DAPO-17k, NuminaMath, DeepScaleR. Average speedup by benchmark: DAPO-1k 3.0x, MATH500 3.5x, AMC2023 3.2x, AIME 3.3x. Example: 7B reaches 0.45 on DAPO-1k in 7.6 h with SPEED-RLOO, vanilla about 3.4x longer. Before filtering, 34% (1.5B) and 25.8% (7B) of 1000 DAPO-17k prompts had pass rate exactly 0. SPEED keeps training accuracy near 0.5.
quote: SPEED achieves target validation accuracies 2-6 times faster compared with baseline RL algorithms
limits: Speedup is time-to-target, not final accuracy. Total rollouts per prompt are held at N (screening N_init plus continuation), so it is not just 'more rollouts'. No separate ablation of mid-pass-rate vs random subset at equal rollouts. Larger N_init (4,6,8) lowered efficiency. Gap 2 partly closed.
agent_relevance: Analogue of 'rising difficulty' for training only; the scaffold does not train.

source: SPEED-RL theory section (Theorem 3.1; rollouts vs selection; reward type)
finding: The paper names the plain alternative: raise SNR by sampling more rollouts per prompt, which is costly. Selection reaches high SNR cheaper. The reward is rule-based in all arms, so verifier choice is not the source of the gain.
numbers: Typical N = 16-64 rollouts per prompt. Baseline and SPEED use the same rule-based reward.
limits: Text and tables read; ablation figures not inspected. Gap 2: verifier confound ruled out within the paper; rollout-count alternative argued, not run as a matched ablation.

source: Suzgun, Yuksekgonul, Bianchi, Jurafsky & Zou (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: test-time learning with adaptive memory
finding: A frozen model that keeps a self-curated text memory across a stream of questions improves, with no labels. Part of the gain comes from better instructions alone (DC- with no memory).
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024: baseline 23.3, DC- (instructions, no memory) 36.7, DC-Cu 50.0, DC-RS 46.7. AIME 2025: 6.7, 23.3, 36.7, 30.0. GPT-4o Game of 24: 10 baseline, 19 DC-, 99 DC-RS (found a Python brute force and reused it). GPQA-Diamond Claude 59.6 to 68.7 (DC-RS); GPT-4o 57.1 flat. MMLU-Pro Engineering GPT-4o 53.2 to 51.2 (no gain).
quote: DC adapts LMs' problem-solving skills on the fly, without modifying their underlying parameters
limits: Single run per cell, small sets (AIME 30 questions). Memory gain over DC- is 13.3 points on AIME 2024 for Claude. Many GPT-4o cells show no gain or a loss. Order effects not ablated.
agent_relevance: Closest published inference-time analogue of practice across tasks. Gains are strongest when tasks share structure.

source: Dynamic Cheatsheet, sections on small models and ordering
finding: Gains need a capable model. Small models (GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3.5 Haiku) and R1/o1 gave little or inconsistent benefit. The authors suggest without testing that easy-first ordering could help.
numbers: Small-model cells in the paper: some DC-Cu and DC-RS results fall below baseline. Text says faulty heuristics that slip into memory can propagate.
quote: curriculum-style learning ... may potentially bootstrap performance
limits: Ordering claim is speculation in the paper. Gap 3 not answered here.
agent_relevance: Memory-writing step needs a strong model; matches schema caution about self-written rules.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: Retrying a task with a stored self-written reflection after a failed attempt raises success within a session, using external signals (test results, environment reward). Closest to within-session repeated practice.
numbers: AlfWorld (134 tasks): +22% absolute over baseline in 12 iterative steps. HotPotQA +20%. HumanEval Python pass@1 80 (GPT-4) to 91.0; HumanEval Rust 60 to 68; MBPP Rust 71 to 75; LeetcodeHard 7.5 to 15.0.
limits: Multi-attempt, so it spends more tokens than one attempt; paper has no equal-token best-of-N control. Gap 1 stays open for equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Feedback-driven retries help only when a signal exists.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion, MBPP Python failure analysis
finding: Boundary condition: when the self-written test is unreliable, the retry loop does worse than no loop. MBPP Python fell from 0.80 to 0.77.
numbers: Test-suite false-positive rate 16.3% on MBPP Python vs 1.4% on HumanEval Python. HumanEval Python base 0.80, Reflexion 0.91.
limits: Shows loop quality is bounded by evaluator quality.
agent_relevance: Supports guardrails that need an external check before trusting a retry.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: An agent that gathers experiences on training tasks, extracts text insights, and retrieves similar trajectories improves on held-out tasks without weight updates. Both abstraction and retrieval matter.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieve-only success: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%, ALFWorld 50% vs 55%, WebShop 37% vs 38%. ExpeL 40% at R3 on HotpotQA vs Reflexion 39%; ALFWorld 54% vs 59% (ExpeL, no repeated attempts). Ablation HotpotQA: full ExpeL 39.0 vs 32.0 with gpt-3.5 insights; ALFWorld random example selection 40.0 vs ExpeL 59.0.
limits: Table rows read from a layout-garbled PDF, some may be misaligned. Task ordering not ablated.
agent_relevance: Insight extraction is a learned-rules step that schema section 4b may rule out.

source: He et al. (2026) EvoTest: evolutionary test-time learning for self-improving agentic systems (ICLR 2026)
finding: Controlled benchmark J-TTL: same game played for K=50 consecutive episodes, no gradients. A static agent stays flat, so plain repetition does nothing; methods that use episode transcripts improve.
numbers: Average AUC (Gemini 2.5 Flash / Claude 4 Sonnet): Static 0.11/0.12, Memory 0.13/0.14, RAG 0.18/0.19, Reflexion 0.32/0.34, TextGrad 0.31/0.33, EvoPrompt 0.34/0.36, GRPO online 0.30, SFT online 0.23, EvoTest 0.47/0.50. Six Jericho games; EvoTest only method to win Detective and Library.
quote: On J-TTL, we find that existing adaptation methods like reflection, memory, or reinforcement learning struggle.
limits: Single-task repeat, not graded difficulty. Compute not token-matched across methods (EvoTest 1 extra LLM call per episode, Reflexion 1). Authors admit strategic overfitting to the instance. Gap 1: yes for repeat-same-task with feedback at similar call count; token-matched control absent.
agent_relevance: In-session learning is possible; the gain comes from rewriting the prompt (w/o Prompt Detective AUC 0.94 to 0.52).

finding: Removing components costs score. Evolver model quality matters. Learned rules are brittle to small changes in the task.
numbers: Detective AUC: full 0.94; w/o Prompt 0.52; w/o UCB 0.68; w/o Memory 0.82; w/o Hyperparameters 0.89; w/o Tool-use 0.91. Evolver LLM: o3 0.94, DeepSeek R1 0.90, Qwen3-32B 0.82, Qwen3-8B 0.68, static 0.21.
limits: Greedy selection without UCB gave catastrophic drops after lucky mutations.
agent_relevance: Matches Dynamic Cheatsheet: a weak model gives weak self-improvement.

source: ReasoningBank and MaTTS: scaling agent self-evolving with reasoning memory (Google Research, 2025)
finding: Compares memory with test-time scaling. More samples without memory give small unstable gains; with memory the same scaling gives larger steady gains. Partial answer to the equal-compute question.
numbers: WebArena pass@1 with scale factor k: MaTTS parallel 49.7 (k=1) to 55.1 (k=5); sequential 49.7 to 54.5. Without memory: parallel 39.0-42.2, sequential 37.4-40.6 (fluctuating). Vanilla TTS (no aggregation) at k=5: 52.4 parallel, 51.9 sequential. Table 1 subset: No Memory 39.0, Synapse 40.6, AWM 44.4; up to 16% fewer steps.
limits: Equal k means equal rollouts between memory and no-memory arms, the nearest thing to an equal-token control found. Web and SWE benchmarks; authors have a stake.
agent_relevance: Memory plus more samples compound; sampling alone does not.

source: Evo-Memory (2025) Benchmarking LLM agent test-time learning with self-evolving memory
finding: Direct test of task ordering in streaming memory. Hard-to-easy order did BETTER than easy-to-hard, the opposite of a rising-difficulty curriculum. Gap 3 answered for this setting.
numbers: AlfWorld/ScienceWorld success (SR): ReMem Easy-to-Hard 0.91 / 0.63 (avg 0.77), Hard-to-Easy 0.94 / 0.68 (avg 0.81); ExpRAG avg 0.57 vs 0.69; ExpRecent 0.57 vs 0.60. Base avg 0.41. AlfWorld steps fell 22.6 to 11.5 with ReMem. Gain tracks task similarity (Pearson .717 on Gemini 2.5 Flash, .563 on Claude 3.7 Sonnet).
limits: Two environments in the ordering test; one ordering per direction; no seed variance given. Authors infer hard-task experience transfers more. Unfiltered failed experiences hurt baselines.
agent_relevance: Task order is a minor lever; similarity matters more.

source: Decocted Experience Improves Test-Time Inference in LLM Agents (2026)
finding: Accumulated experience helps only if distilled into lessons and kept at moderate size; more raw experience is not better.
numbers: Findings: lesson distillation beats raw trajectories on agentic tasks; performance has a sweet spot at intermediate memory size that beats full memory; best context balances relevance and diversity. Tasks: math, web browsing, SWE.
limits: Abstract, intro and findings list read; figure values not extracted.
agent_relevance: Supports pruning in any memory-using scaffold.
